## Introduction

### The Task
The goal of this project is to look at the environmental impact because homes built before and after 1930. This report will also build a model to be able to accurately predict when a home was built based off of the environmental impact data. This will be beneficial because it will allow officials to approach these homes with a different strategy that is needed for reducing the environmental impact of UK housing. 

### The Problem
Climate change is an every increasing issue in the world and it is important to reduce the amount of carbon emissions in all aspects of life, including housing. Since housing has a multitude of variables that impacts it's energy efficiency and carbon footprint, it makes sense that a different approach to reduce the environmental impact will be different for different types of homes. Homes can be separated out into two groups, homes built before 1930 and homes built after. This makes sense because older homes were built differently and are more settled so drafts are more of an issue. 

The data used in this report is a non-random sample of UK housing from [Energy Certificates](https://epc.opendatacommunities.org/) and was downloaded December of 2025. The full dataset is only available on server '10.121.4.250' with the file 'energy.energy_certificates'. There are 93 total variables which include information on: 

- Property energy efficiency -- the data provides a ranking from A (most efficient) to G (least efficient)
- CO~2~ Emissions
- Electricity costs

The goal of this report is to determine if it is possible to categorize how old a home is (pre and post 1930) based off of energy efficiency data and the metrics: `current_energy_efficiency`, `environment_impact_current`, `energy_consumption_current`, `co2_emissions_current`, `lighting_cost_current`, `heating_cost_current`, `hot_water_cost_current`. If able to predict the age of the home based off of the data will save a lot of resources because having a home visit to gather that information would not be needed.

## Fitting LDA and QDA classifiers

The simplest classifiers we could apply are Linear and Quadratic Discriminant analysis (LDA and QDA respectively). LDA uses Bayes' theorem to calculate the probability if an input will belong to a specific output grouping. QDA is a more complex method that is similar to LDA but additionally uses its own covariance matrix. Both methods are extremely useful; however, sometimes over complicating the model can do more harm than good. Therefore, it is best to compare the two models to determine which one is the better fit for predicting the age of a home. 

### Results from fitting a linear discriminant analysis

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| results: 'asis'
df = pd.read_csv('../../data_cache/vignettes/supervised_classification/lda.csv')
df.rename(columns={"Unnamed: 0": "Category"}, inplace=True)
print(df.round(3).to_markdown(index=False))
```

### Results from fitting a quadratic discriminant analysis

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| results: 'asis'
df = pd.read_csv('../../data_cache/vignettes/supervised_classification/qda.csv')
df.rename(columns={"Unnamed: 0": "Category"}, inplace=True)
print(df.round(3).to_markdown(index=False))
```

Precision relates to how many positives the model was able to correctly identify. This does not take into account the number of false positives. Where LDA has a more even precision between positively identifying homes built before and after 1930. QDA has a harder time identifying correctly more modern homes but is much better at determining older homes. This means that the QDA model is more likely to classify a home has being older.  


The confusion matrices below allow for a better visualization of how well each model works. Where TP is 'true positive', FP is 'false positive', FN is 'false negative', and TN is 'true negative'. This has a much more clear display that QDA has three times greater number of false positives than LDA. On the other hand, LDA has double the amount of false negatives than QDA has. These two models have their pros and cons however with further analysis, it can be determined which model is best for the task at hand.

![](../../data_cache/vignettes/supervised_classification/confusion_matrix_LDA.html){width="100%" height="300px"}
![](../../data_cache/vignettes/supervised_classification/confusion_matrix_QDA.html){width="100%" height="300px"}


## ROC curve and AUC for two simple classifiers

The Receiver Operating Characteristic or ROC curve is a model that determines how reliable the model is at differentiating between two classifiers. True Positive Rate (TPR) is the proportion of how many times the model is correct in identifying a positive case as such. Conversely, False Positive Rate (FPR) is the proportion of cases that are negative but where identified as positive. 

The Area Under the Curve (ACU) is an index that determines how well the model is. The scale goes from 0-1 where 1 is perfect and 0.5 is random and anything less than 0.5 is worse than if the model was truly random.

![](../../data_cache/vignettes/supervised_classification/roc.html){width="100%" height="600px"}

Here it can be seen that the performance of the LDA classifier has an AUC of 0.81 and the QDA classifier as a AUC of 0.79. Both of these models are fairly good, however the LDA is slightly better and should be used to determine if homes are built before or after 1930.
